Me, Old Ji, and Forty-Two—we each put down one attestation, and not one of us can get away. But remember this: this half hour of waiting was never to hide from responsibility. It was to press the loss into the accounts. Think of it the other way around: if I’m quick with my hands today and judge it good, then issue it out, and tomorrow it goes bad in someone’s belly, that is what you call truly counting it against someone’s head. Against the family who ate it, and against me, Lin Zhao. As it is now, the worst is no more than one extra sound in the basket. One sound in exchange for one belly—that trade is no loss.”

“There are also people muttering in their hearts: if we balance the accounts today, how can they be balanced with the word ‘pending’ hanging there?” I opened the ledger and showed that page to the doorway. “Look here. Three columns: good, bad, pending inspection. Add the three columns together, and they equal the total inspected, not one piece off—that is balanced. ‘Pending’ is also a number. Once it falls into ink, it is no longer hanging. Tomorrow morning, when the cloth is dry, if it turns good, it enters the accounts and goes with the next round; if the cloth is wet, it goes into the basket and the bad count gains one entry. The front and back pages bite into each other; it can’t run away.”

I lifted my chin toward the woman at the doorway. “You come first thing tomorrow morning. The cloth was laid out while you watched me, and the circle was drawn in front of you. You watch with your own eyes which column this entry is moved into from ‘pending,’ then check it against the pillar, and the pillar against the basket. When all three places bite together, this tin will have a beginning and an end.”

The fingernails she had dug into the doorframe stopped, and she slowly nodded.

Thunder rolled over the roof of the shed again; the rain hammered the oilcloth with puffing sounds. Old Ji pressed the umbrella another half inch lower. I put the second tin of the fourth rack back into Forty-Two’s hands. His hands were red from the cold, but his eyes were still bright.

“If the questions are finished, then get to work. Before dark, every tin’s whereabouts must fall into one of the three columns.”

“Keep calling.”
“…Th-then those cans awaiting inspection—if they really seep water by tomorrow morning, who’s that on?!”

This sentence came in stepping on the thunder. Forty-two’s hand paused for half a breath on the second can, and he looked up at me. I nodded to him: keep counting.

He pressed down, turned it over, checked the seam, and called, “Fourth rack, second can, good!”

“Record it.” I set my brush down; the three ledgers matched. “Good thirty, bad fifteen, awaiting inspection one. Forty-six counted.”

Only then did I lift my eyes toward the door. The one asking was not the woman from before. She had shifted half a step to the side, her mouth still moving, and behind her a new face had squeezed forward, trouser legs wet to the knees. He had run through the rain from the line to take shelter under the eaves, with two or three more faces pressing behind him.

The same question had been asked twice within the time it takes an incense stick to burn. In my line of work, this is how you put it: if every time an account is raised, someone comes to check it, and every time it has to be recalculated, then you should not be recalculating it in front of people every time. You should set a rule. And there was another layer that was my fault: the answer I gave just now was too long. Once the thunder rolled, it broke off; by the time it reached the third person’s ears, only half of it was left. Half an answer grates more than no answer at all.

“All of you come in under the eaves. Don’t stand in the rain asking about accounts.” I beckoned toward the doorway. “This question is being asked a second time, and I am not angry. If you are willing to ask, it means you are looking at the accounts and thinking. That is a good thing. The problem is on my side: my answer was long, and the rain can wash it away. This time I’ll give you the short version, short enough that the rain can’t wash it away.”

I held up two fingers.

“Twelve words, two sentences.”

“Shortfall: count it under the rain’s account.”

“Miscount: count it under the signers’ account.”

“The first sentence: if it really seeps through by tomorrow morning, it goes into the basket, and the bad count gets another entry. Everyone will be able to see it on the pillar by evening. But it has never gone into anyone’s bowl, never gone onto anyone’s turn; it cannot take up anyone’s quota, and cannot crowd out anyone’s turn. This loss is recorded under the name of last night’s rain.”

“The second sentence: three ledgers, three signatures—mine, Old Ji’s, and Forty-two’s, one each, black ink on white paper. If it truly was inspected wrong, then tomorrow morning we find people by those signatures. Not one can get away.”

“If you cannot remember the long version, then carry these twelve words with you. Go home and tell your families; let your families tell the neighbors. From now on, if anyone asks this question again, there is no need to brave the rain and crowd to the warehouse door. You will be carrying the answer in your own mouths.”

Giving it only by mouth was still not enough. I opened the notes at the very front of the ledger, the old method handed down from the grain station before the disaster: new rules are first entered in the notes, then in the running account. I lifted my brush and, in front of the several pairs of eyes at the door, wrote:

Cans awaiting inspection: cloth dry, enter as good; cloth wet, enter as bad. Those that turn bad are recorded under the rain account, not under any person’s account and not under any turn. If inspection is wrong, the three signers bear it together.

After writing it, I pointed to the words and read them slowly once, so that even those who could not read would take them into their ears.

“This rule is not being set only for the can in front of us. From now on, any can we are unsure about will be handled according to this. Set the rule once, and it saves answering again every time. Tonight this rule will also be copied onto the pillar, nailed up together with the turns and the bad count.”

“You, the one who asked just now.” I nodded at that unfamiliar face. “These twelve words—shout them once to the people behind you. Once you shout them out, this answer belongs to all of you, not to my counter.”

He froze for half a breath, then craned his neck and shouted out, “Shortfall—count it under the rain’s account! Miscount—count it under the signers’ account!” His voice cracked, but it carried. Under the eaves, people followed and recited it, one sentence biting into the next, mixed with the rain as it moved toward the end of the line. My throat could not outrun this rain; two hundred mouths could.

Old Ji lowered the umbrella another half inch. In the charcoal circle, that can was still upside down; the clean corner of oilcloth was still clean. The time had not come; there was no rushing it. It would reveal itself.

Forty-two’s hands were frozen red, but his eyes were still bright.

I took down the third can from the fourth rack and set it into his palm.

“All right. The long answer and the short answer are both complete. Each of you keep them well.”

“Third can. Keep calling.”
“Fourth shelf, third can—the lid is good, and the seam is dry too... but Lin Zhao, why is the date printed on the bottom of this can even earlier than last month?!”

Forty-Two held the can toward me bottom-up. I did not answer right away; first I ran it through my hands: pressed the lid with my fingertip—no pop; flipped it over, felt along the welded seam inch by inch—clean; tilted it and counted to ten—the seam did not raise a single bead. Only after it had passed all three checks did I bring the bottom into that strip of light by the door and squint at the line of stamped steel lettering.

Once I had looked, I knew what to do. This question was even more worth pausing over than that cry of “rusted through.” A swollen lid and seepage—everyone knew that meant bad. But the three words “old date” were something everyone understood, yet no one was quite sure about; they were the easiest thing to ride the sound of the rain and burrow into people’s hearts. If I did not catch that tone first, before the notices were even pasted on the pillars tonight, the sentence “the East Storehouse is hoarding expired old stock” would have run through the whole station. That would hurt people more than the number of bad cans.

“Good eyes. You even turned it over to look at the bottom.” First I acknowledged what he had seen. “But those eyes looked in the wrong place. Listen to the reasoning, and when I’m done you can judge for yourself.”

“Canned goods are not made with the expectation that people will rush to eat them the day they leave the factory. Before the disaster I kept accounts at the grain station. There was an old saying passed down over the counter: the date is its birthday; the seal is its life. When you check a household register, you check the birthday; when you inspect goods, you inspect the life.”

“Before the disaster, cans were printed with ‘best quality for three years.’ That was the manufacturer’s wording. What it guaranteed was that within three years the taste would not suffer and the manufacturer would take responsibility. It did not mean that once three years were up, it turned into poison. If you really want to talk about the poison line, there is only one: did dirty water get in or not. Whether it got in is not determined by what year it was born in, but by whether the seal has confessed. It confesses in three ways: swollen lid, seepage, rusted-through. The ones lying in the basket have all confessed. This one,” I raised it and waved it toward the door, “has a flat lid, a dry seam, and does not pop when pressed. It has not confessed.”

“Let me reckon another figure for you.” I raised my voice over the rain on the eaves. “From the disaster to today, it has been a full seven years. In these seven years, which can that has gone into anyone’s belly did not have a pre-disaster date? If we really counted by that old paper from before the disaster, every can in the station ought to go into the basket. Then what has everyone been eating these seven years? The ones that really caused trouble—when we checked afterward, every single time it was because the seal was broken. Not once was the date to blame.”

“As for why its date is earlier than last month’s, the source is different.” I set the can back on the table. “What you saw last month was newly dug ruin-stock brought in by the patrol team. Whatever batch they dug up was what we got. Some shops had just restocked a few days before the disaster, so the dates were ‘recent.’ This batch from the East Storehouse is old reserve stock, accumulated in the first few years. When it was stored, no one looked at the date; they looked at the seal. Old is its provenance, not its illness.”

“But that glance of yours has reminded me. From now on we add half a rule: when handling each can, glance at the year while you’re at it. Don’t enter it in the good-or-bad column; just call it out. If the years in any stack cluster together, call it out, so we can figure out what year this reserve stock came in. After the count is done, I’ll turn up the old warehouse pages and compare the source; whatever matches, I’ll write down. For those that don’t, the list will carry the four words ‘source pending investigation.’ Same principle as that can set upside down: leaving it hanging and unspoken is the hole; once it falls into ink, it no longer hangs.”

I glanced toward the corner of the oilcloth. The can inside the charcoal circle was still upside down, and the cloth was still dry. Its time had not come; there was no need to rush. It would confess on its own.

“Those at the door, record ten words: the date is its birthday; the seal is its life. Pass that on when you go home.”

“This can,” I looked back at Forty-Two, “you pressed it and felt it; I checked it again. All three checks are complete. Report.”

His throat bobbed, and he called out: “Fourth rack, third can, good!”

“Record it.” The three ledgers matched tightly. “Good thirty-one, bad fifteen, awaiting inspection one. Counted forty-seven.”

In my heart I weighed that fifteen. Out of forty-seven cans, fifteen bad—just over thirty percent. That number was heavy, but heavy was better than hanging—hanging meant having no number; heavy meant having a number. The counting was not finished, and I would not allow myself to collapse first.

Thunder rolled across the shed roof, and Old Ji pressed the umbrella another half inch over the account book. I placed the fourth can from the fourth rack into Forty-Two’s cold-reddened palms.

“Keep going. Glance at the year while you’re at it, but don’t hold up the count.”
“Fourth rack, fourth can—lid is good, seam is dry... but Lin Zhao, the weld on the bottom of this can is crooked! Did it leak air?!”

I take that can from him. I do not speak at first; my hands go over it first: press the lid, no spring; trace the weld seam to the end with my fingertips, dry, with no rust spots and no damp line. Crooked it is, truly crooked—that seam does not run down the center, but slants off by nearly half a finger’s width.

But I am in no hurry to call the count.

“First, I’ll grant your eye for this: crooked, yes, truly crooked.” I lift the can into the strip of light at the doorway and turn it half a circle, letting everyone under the eaves see clearly. “Now look at this one.”

From the scrap basket I pick out the can whose bottom is rusted through; the muddy water has long since drained dry. I hold both cans up together. The woman at the doorway cranes her neck and looks over both seams.

“This can’s seam runs perfectly straight, straighter and neater than any other, but there is a rusted hole in the bottom. That can’s seam is crooked by half a finger, but the seal is tight all the way around. Whether it lives or dies is not in its appearance, but in whether the seal has failed.”

“Why is the seam crooked? It isn’t an injury; it came that way from the making. The factory machine pressed off-center that day, and it came out crooked. If a crooked seam is sealed, it stays sealed; if a straight seam has rusted through, then it is through. Crooked is an appearance, not a crime.”

“As for the leak you asked about: if air had really leaked in, the bacteria outside would have gotten inside, the contents would have spoiled, and once they spoiled they would have produced gas. The gas would push up the lid, and when you pressed it down it would spring back. It does not spring back when pressed, which means air has never gotten in.”

“However,” I pause, “with a crooked seam, I am right to be half a measure more suspicious. Once the seam is crooked, the stress on the seal is uneven, and the thin places are more delicate than elsewhere. So it has to pass one more test than the others.”

With my thumbnail, I scrape along that crooked seam from one end to the other. Fingertips feel the surface; a fingernail scrapes the line—a crack as fine as a strand of hair may not be felt by the fingertip gliding over it, but a nail will catch on it. I scrape to the end; it does not catch. Then I tilt it and count several tens of beats. Not a single bead emerges from the seam.

“It has passed all four tests, but I still won’t rule it good.” I wipe it dry with a cloth, turn it upside down, and draw a second charcoal circle on the oilcloth, side by side with the first. “Damage is something the eyes can see, and can be judged on the spot; a hidden risk is something the eyes cannot see, and must be handed over to time.”

I pick up the brush and add a line to the general notes: All cans with crooked seams, even if they pass the four tests, are to be inverted and held for inspection; if the cloth is dry, enter as good; if the cloth is wet, enter as bad. After writing it, I slowly read it aloud once for those at the doorway to hear.

“Record it. Fourth rack, fourth can: crooked seam, held for inspection. Make the three books match.” I call to the general ledger. “Good thirty-one, bad fifteen, pending inspection two. Forty-eight counted. Everyone listen: don’t only count the bad book. There are thirty-one good ones now. Record both books together. Don’t let the bad accounts swallow the good ones.”

Someone at the doorway mutters, “How is there another one pending inspection……”

“Pending inspection isn’t bad; it just has one extra hurdle in its fate.” I answer that person. “There are two cans lying on the oilcloth now. Tomorrow morning, in the time it takes an incense stick to burn, the cloth will speak for us. If you think that’s too slow, think of the other end of it: if I move fast and call it good, and it’s issued to someone’s household, and in the middle of the night that family’s child is holding it and vomiting, will you still think I was too slow then?”

Forty-two casually reports a year, and I write it in the margin of the page, to check it tonight against the old warehouse entry pages for its source. I glance at the first charcoal circle; the cloth is still dry. That it has shown no failure by now is a good sign. But signs do not go into the account; only numbers do.

I look at Forty-two again. From the fourth rack onward, this boy has been able to pick out something wrong with every can: bulging lid, water seepage, the sound of water, old date, crooked seam. His eyes are getting sharper and sharper, and the person himself is growing more and more taut.

“Let me say something off the subject.” I place the fifth can into his frost-reddened hands, but do not let him call it yet. “Suspicion has no bottom; rules have a bottom. If you rely only on suspicion, you can count until dark and still not finish; at night you’ll sleep with your eyes open. Hand suspicion over to the rules: four tests, inverted holding, three books cross-checked. Let the rules suspect on your behalf. You only need to follow the procedure. Once the procedure is complete, whatever fate it has is the fate it has. It is not yours to stew over.”

“Every thing you picked out today has gone into the general notes. From now on, when Huiling counts cans again, every item will have a rule to follow. You are not nitpicking for me; you are setting rules for the next seven years.”

Thunder rolls over the shed roof again. Slanting flecks of rain blow in. I brace the ledger with my back, and Old Ji presses the umbrella low.

“Fifth can. Keep calling.”
“Fourth rack, fifth tin—the lid is good, the seam is dry too... but Lin Zhao, this tin makes no sound when you shake it! Is it empty inside?!”

I took that can from him and said nothing at first. First, I weighed it in my hand.

Supporting the bottom with one hand, I bounced it up and down twice. Heavy, pressing into the hand. I already had seventy or eighty percent of the answer in mind, then picked out from the good-goods pile a passed can of similar size, and held one in each hand, level, like a steelyard.

“Stop using your ears. Use your hands.” I put both cans into Forty-two’s hands. “Left hand, the one you said makes no sound; right hand, the one that passed. Weigh them.”

He weighed them, then weighed them again, and his brow loosened half a degree. “...The left hand is even a bit heavier.”

“Lao Ji, you weigh it too.” Three pairs of hands were the same principle as three sets of accounts.

Only after Lao Ji also nodded did I speak. “A shaking sound is the sound of spare liquid. Canned fish soaks in brine, canned fruit soaks in syrup; there is liquid inside that sloshes, so it rattles. But luncheon meat, minced meat, that line of goods, they’re packed solid and tight, without a drop of spare liquid. If you shake it, what is it supposed to make sound with? It isn’t empty. It’s so full there’s no room to sound.”

“Now weigh another account. A can that has truly leaked empty has only a layer of iron shell left, light as an empty tin box. This one presses the hand, and is even half a bit heavier than the one that passed. With cans, the ears can fool people; weight does not. If it doesn’t rattle, maybe it’s solid; if it feels light, then it is truly empty.”

“But solid has its own way of checking; you have to give it one more careful look than the others.” I pressed my fingertip onto the lid. “It has no spare liquid to leak. If a hole really let air in, once the stuff inside spoils it will produce gas, and the gas will push up the lid. So for a solid can, the lid-pressing step is the most important. You pressed it just now; I’ll press it again.” I pressed down; it did not spring at all. “One more precaution: if it really seeped and then dried in the shade, residue will be left along the seam, sticky to the touch.” I wiped along the seam to the end and rubbed my fingers together. “Dry and clean, not sticky.”

“Equal weight, flat lid, clean seam, no residue: all four are present. Report.”

His throat bobbed. “Fourth rack, fifth can, good!”

“Record it.” The three books bit together. “Good thirty-two, bad fifteen, pending inspection two. Forty-nine counted.”

I raised my brush and added another line to the conventions: For any silent can, first weigh it, then inspect the seal. If equal in weight to good goods, it is solid; handle by the usual rule. If light in the hand, check for residue and transfer to pending inspection. After writing it, I slowly read it out for the doorway to hear.

“Those at the door, remember twelve words: whether it rattles is temperament; whether it is heavy is conscience. Take that home and pass it on.”

Someone under the eaves muttered, “The goods on this rack are uncanny; listen close and they’ve got things to say...” Laughter spread. The woman’s fingernails, gripping the doorframe, loosened for the first time.

I waited until the laughter had fallen by half before continuing. “Laughing is laughing, accounting is accounting. The things he picked out along the way—water sounds, old dates, crooked seams, no sound—today every one of them has gone into the conventions. From now on, when Huiling opens a storehouse again, whoever counts cans will have to follow the methods he picked out.”

In my heart I weighed this lad. In one morning, he had gone from fault-finder to appraiser. Suspicion put in the right place is a craft.

I glanced at that corner of the oilcloth: two charcoal circles side by side, the cloth still dry. The time had not come; they would reveal themselves. The thunder, however, had moved half a step farther off; the rain was still dense. As for Heaven’s temper, I did not dare judge it good in advance. Until all the numbers are finished, I won’t acknowledge anyone’s good.

Forty-two reported a year in passing, and I recorded it in the margin. I put the sixth can into his frost-reddened palm. The way he weighed the can already looked proper.

“Sixth can. Keep calling them out.”
"Fourth rack, sixth tin—the lid is good, the seam is dry, there is sound when shaken... But Lin Zhao, why is there a scratch on the bottom of this tin? Was it dropped?!"

I took that can, and first went through the old three checks: press the lid, no spring; feel the seam, dry; tilt it and count off several dozen, no beads appeared at the seam. Only then did I turn the bottom over and bring that scratch into the strip of light at the doorway.

One line, slanting across just under half a finger, shallow, its edges darkened.

“First, to answer what you asked: was it dropped?” I turned the bottom half a circle toward the doorway so everyone under the eaves could see. “If it was dropped, that means smashed. The wound from a smash is a dent—a sunken patch, a piece of paint flaked off, with squeezed-up wrinkles along the edge. A scrape is what leaves a line. This line was scraped: the can was in the patrol team’s bag, on the rack, iron rubbing iron. After seven years, wearing out a line like this isn’t strange.”

“A drop leaves a dent; a scrape leaves a line. Those at the door, remember those eight words, and I’ll give you five more: it hurts the skin, not the life.”

“There’s another layer. Look at this exposed edge.” I pointed at that bit of darkness inside the scratch. “It’s darkened, which means it’s an old wound. The iron has been exposed for some days. It wasn’t newly scraped last night. Don’t put it on the rain’s account; put it on the road’s account. Seven years of hauling left its mark on it.”

“But a scratch is a scratch. Whether it lives or dies depends on whether the vital part was hurt. This time, you do it yourself.” I handed the can back. “Use your fingernail and scrape along this line from one end to the other. If it catches hard, it’s a groove and the tin has been pierced; if it slides over or only catches a little, it’s a skin wound. Scrape.”

Forty-Two set his nail to it and scraped very slowly, once, then again, and looked up. “…It only catches a little.”

“I’ll recheck.” I scraped once. Same result. “Now look where it fell: the center of the bottom, one solid piece of iron. Those lying in the basket, go count them later—which one died at the center of the bottom? They all died at the seams, at the holes. The fatal wounds always land on the seal.”

“But with that one look, you’ve caught another matter.” I pointed at the dark exposed iron in the scratch. “The paint’s been scraped off, and the iron is exposed like this. Leave it three or five months, and it’ll rust on its own. A can like this is good today, but it can’t be stored long.”

I raised my brush and added a line to the general rules: For scratched cans: shallow and not reaching the seam, enter as good as usual; deep groove or crossing the seam, invert and await inspection; exposed iron, though good, enter the rotation first. After writing it, I read it aloud for the people at the door.

“Listen carefully to the words ‘enter the rotation first.’ Tonight, when the turns are posted on the pillar, put the wounded ones at the front and issue them first. While they’re still good goods, move them out first. If you leave them to the end, a skin wound will stew into a real wound, and good goods will stew into goods for the basket.”

“Report.”

His throat bobbed. “Fourth rack, sixth can, good!”

“Record it.” The three ledgers matched. “Good thirty-three, bad fifteen, pending inspection two—we’ve counted fifty.”

I called out that fifty a bit more heavily. The woman at the doorway lifted her head, and I nodded to her. “Fifty cans entered into account; thirty-three are good. Bad accounts are being entered one by one, and the good accounts haven’t been idle either. Both ledgers are being kept.”

Someone under the eaves picked up the thread. “The goods on this rack each come with a story…”

“Stories aren’t frightening,” I answered. “Once a story enters the general rules, it becomes a rule; what doesn’t enter the general rules is the real disaster. What he picked out today—water sound, old date, crooked seam, no sound, scratch—five types. From now on, anyone opening the storehouse has to follow every one of them.”

I glanced at that corner of the oilcloth. Two charcoal circles sat side by side; the cloth was still dry. The thunder had drawn another half-step farther away, and the rain was still dense, but it was no longer striking quite so hard. Heaven seemed to have let out half a breath. I did not acknowledge it. Until the count was finished, not even the sky’s expression counted.

Forty-Two reported the year, and I recorded it in the page margin. A bit of rust had rubbed into the cracks around his fingernails, and the way he weighed the can was much steadier than it had been in the morning.

I set the seventh can into his frost-reddened palm.

“Seventh can. Keep calling.”
"Fourth rack, seventh can—the lid is good, the seam is dry... but Lin Zhao, this can sounds wrong when you shake it! Why's it like there's sand mixed in?!"

I had just reached out to take it when a voice burst out first from the doorway: it was the woman from East Sixth Row, clinging to the doorframe and shouting, “Heft it first! Whether it rattles is temperament; whether it has weight is conscience!”

My hand stopped in midair. Those twelve words were what I had thrown out that morning, and now they were using them to judge a case. Once words grow into two hundred mouths, they are no longer my words; they are Huiling’s own rules.

“What she shouted is the right path.” I lifted my chin toward Forty-Two. “If the ears raise suspicion, let the hands decide. Of all the cans you’ve hefted today, you’ve heard more than anyone. This time, you do it.”

From the pile of good goods, I picked out a can of similar size that had passed inspection and set it together with the one in his hand. He hefted one in each hand. At first his brow was relaxed; then it tightened hard. He hefted them again. On the third time, he looked up, his voice tense:

“Uncle Lin… the one in my left hand is light.”

I passed it through my hands too, and so did Old Ji. Three pairs of hands were the same principle as three ledgers. Light—it was truly light. That missing bit of weight made the string in my heart sink with it. There are only two sources for a sandy rattle: one is that the goods themselves are loose kernels—corn, beans, mixed vegetables—soaked in broth, and when shaken, the kernels rub against each other. That is the type of goods, not a sickness. The other is that the broth has gone, leaving a can of dry kernels rubbing by themselves. To distinguish these two paths, there is only one word: weight.

“First I’ll answer that question about ‘sand mixed in.’” I raised my voice toward the doorway. “For outside sand to get in, the hole would have to be bigger than a grain of sand; if the hole were really that big, last night’s rain would already have filled its belly, and this morning the seam should be hanging with broth. Its seam is dry. Sand didn’t get in. The broth leaked out.”

“If the broth left, it must have left footprints. Fingernail—scrape along the seam. Don’t miss an inch.”

Forty-Two scraped very slowly. Near one corner at the bottom seam, his fingernail stopped. “Here… it catches.”

I took it and brought it into the strip of light at the doorway: a rust spot the size of a sesame seed, with a faint white trace beside it, like a salt stain—the mark of broth having passed there and then dried. Old Ji wiped his hands, checked it, and nodded.

“It has confessed.” I raised that can and turned it half a circle toward the doorway. “Someone may ask: why isn’t the lid bulging? The hole is small, the broth leaked slowly, and the gas hasn’t built up enough to push the lid yet. But if the hole is there, it’s doomed. If it doesn’t die today and muddles through, it will die in the pot of the household whose turn it reaches. Record it in all three ledgers: fourth rack, seventh can, concealed leakage from a rust hole, condemned.”

With a clang, it dropped into the basket.

“You all saw it.” I pointed at the woman by the doorway. “Those twelve words just now were shouted by her. After she shouted them, the very first case ran straight into her words. From now on, learn this saying from her. No need to wait for me.”

She froze against the doorframe for a long time. Her fingernails loosened, and she forced out a sentence: “I… I was just saying what I remembered from this morning…” Low laughter spread under the shed; this time, the laughter was not hollow.

“I’ll say what’s making you all mutter in your hearts: if broth can quietly leak away, are the other cans also quietly leaking?” I looked around. “That is why every single can passes through hands, through three ledgers, through three sign-offs—not just spot checks. No matter how hidden the leak is, weight does not deceive people, rust spots do not deceive people. The two cans turned upside down on the oilcloth follow the same principle: eyes can be fooled; time cannot.”

I lifted the brush and added a line to the general rules: For all cans with a sandy rattle: first heft for equal weight. Those of equal weight are loose-content goods; inspect the seal as usual. Those that heft light are to have the seam searched for residue; if residue is found, condemn at once; if no residue is found, invert and await inspection. After writing it, I slowly read it aloud for the doorway to hear.

“Remember a new saying, twelve words: if the sound is loose, ask the goods type; if it hefts light, ask whether it lives or dies. Take it home and pass it on.”

“Report the total ledger. Good, thirty-three; bad, sixteen; awaiting inspection, two. Counted through, fifty-one. One entry has been added to the bad account; the thirty-three good entries have not lost a single one. Record both ledgers together.”

Forty-Two stared at the fingernail with which he had scraped out the rust, not moving for a long time. All morning, he had gone from nitpicker to examiner; today, for the first time, his ears had judged a real case.

“This case began with your ears,” I said. “Suspicion placed in the right spot is a craft. Today, every bit of your suspicion was in the right place.”

I glanced at the corner of the oilcloth. Two charcoal circles sat side by side, and the cloth was still dry. The rain had loosened a little, and the thunder had retreated to the west. Whether Heaven relents or not, I don’t recognize it—until the count is finished, even the sky’s expression does not count.

I set the eighth can into his frost-reddened palm.

“The eighth can. Keep calling.”
“Fourth shelf, eighth can—the lid is good, the seam is dry... but Lin Zhao, why is there a lump of black mud stuck to the bottom of this can? Was it soaked in dirty water?!”

I took the can from him, and instead of going through the same old three checks, I first asked, “This can—which cubby did you take it from?”

Forty-two turned back to look at the shelf. “The lower level, the cubby right against the ground.”

“That matches.” I turned the bottom of the can half a circle toward the doorway, letting those under the eaves see that patch of dry, hardened black mud clearly. “First, to answer your question: has it been soaked? Yes. This mud is the confession. Last night the water ran down along the shelf legs and collected in a thin layer on the ground. This lower cubby sits right against the ground, so it was sitting in the water. When the water receded and the mud dried, it bit fast onto the bottom. I said this morning that spoilage has its own ways, following the water. This patch of mud is a road marker left on the waterway. With that one look, you caught the water’s footprints.”

“But having been soaked doesn’t mean it’s bad.” I set the words down steadily before continuing. “The year before the disaster, there was a great flood. The grain station warehouse flooded up to the ankles, and whole racks of cans sat in muddy soup. We fished them out, wiped them dry, inspected the seals can by can, and the ones that passed were issued as usual. That year, nothing happened from eating them. Whether water-soaked cans can be eaten is not something I heard from others; I checked them with my own hands. Cans are born to fight water: iron shells, welded seams, sealing in that one breath of air. If the seal is intact, the water outside can soak it for a year and still not get in. It took a bath; it didn’t drink water.”

“But among soaked cans, there’s one kind of sickness that’s the most insidious. I have to spell it out for you.” I paused. “It’s called water exchange. If the hole is as small as a needle tip, then while it sat in the water for half the night, the dirty water outside could seep in thread by thread through that hole. Once water has been exchanged, the three old pieces of evidence all stop working: the lid doesn’t bulge, because the gas takes days to build up; there’s no stain on the seam, because the moment a stain starts to show, a warehouseful of water has already washed it clean; and when you heft it, it’s neither light nor heavy—how much got exchanged in, how much leaked out, you can’t tell on a rough scale. The scene of this case was destroyed by the rainwater’s own hands.”

“So the old three checks aren’t enough. What a rough scale can’t decide goes to fine examination.” I handled it as usual: press the lid—no springing back; scrape a fingernail along the seam to the end—nothing catches; heft the weight—about the same as good stock. Then I took a bamboo strip and peeled that patch of mud off in one whole piece, close against the bottom.

Under the mud, a layer of yellow rust had risen on the tin. I wiped it with a dry cloth, and it came off. “You all saw that. Mud is a mattress that stores water; the rust took advantage of the damp to show its face. This is why mud-stained cans have to be peeled and checked on the spot. Leave them alone, and floating rust can stew into real rust.”

Old Ji leaned in close and sniffed that piece of mud. “Smells fishy. It’s floor soil from our own storehouse.”

“Right. It isn’t dirt brought back from outside. When it entered the storehouse, it was clean. This bath was taken last night in our own place.”

After wiping it clean, I turned it upside down and drew a third charcoal circle on a clean corner of the oilcloth, side by side with the first two. Three circles lay there; tomorrow morning, in the time it takes one stick of incense to burn, the truth would show on the cloth. That one stick of incense now pressed on the fate of three cans, and also on the sleep of half the station.

I lifted the brush and added a line to the general rules: For all mud-stained cans: peel off the mud and inspect the seal. If the seal is intact, invert and await inspection; if the cloth stays dry, enter as good; if the cloth is wet, enter as bad. For those once soaked in water, stains are insufficient as evidence; judge by the cloth. When I finished writing, I slowly read it aloud for the people at the doorway.

“Those at the doorway, remember twelve words: mud is the water’s road marker; cloth is the leak’s judge. Pass it on when you go home.”

“Record it in all three books: fourth rack, eighth can, mud-stained, awaiting inspection.” I called to the general ledger, “Good thirty-three, bad sixteen, pending inspection three. Counted fifty-two.”

Someone under the eaves muttered, “Why add another pending one again…”

“One more awaiting inspection doesn’t mean one more bad can; it means one more under examination,” I answered. “The first two circles—the cloth is still dry for now. Tomorrow morning, the three cans will go to trial together, and the cloth will confess for them. If there really is a leak, better it leak onto oilcloth than into someone’s family pot. The old rule doesn’t change: if it turns bad, enter it in the rain account; if the inspection is wrong, the three of us shoulder it.”

“One more word for whoever takes these in the future: if a mud-stained can is entered as good, wipe the bottom clean with a cloth before opening it. Keep the outside dirt outside; don’t let it fall into the bowl.”

Forty-two stared at the piece of mud in my hand for a long while, then lowered his head to look at that bit of rust he had rubbed into the cracks of his fingernails in the morning. This kid, when looking at cans now, would turn them over to check the bottom first, then look at the lid.

The rain had gone from pounding to sifting; the thunder had retreated behind the mountains to the west, and that sheet of white along the eaves was no longer so fierce. Whether the sky would relent or not, I did not look at the sky. I looked at the racks. There were still several left; it would only be over when the counting was done.

I placed the ninth can into his frost-reddened palm.

“For the rest on the lower level, turn them over first and check for mud. If there’s mud, handle them according to this can’s procedure.”

“Ninth can. Keep calling.”
“Fourth rack, ninth canister—no mud on the bottom, the lid’s good, the seam’s dry too... but Lin Zhao, why is this canister a whole bit lighter than the others?!”

I took that can from him, and this time I did not start with the same old three checks. I asked first, “Which can did you compare it to?”

Forty-two froze. “To… to the few cans that just passed through my hands.”

“Then this ‘light’ does not count for now.” From the pile of good stock I picked out a standard-sized can, set it beside the one in his hand on the oilcloth, and pushed them into the strip of light at the doorway. “Look for yourself.”

It was half a finger shorter, its body a whole ring narrower. Several heads poked in under the eaves; once they saw clearly, laughter broke out with a buzz.

“All morning, your eyes have been nailed to the lids, the seams, the bottoms, and not one of you remembered the size,” I said. “In this trade, the eyes judge life or death, and the hands judge weight. This can—your eyes have already checked whether it lives or dies, and your hands also caught the weight for you. Your hands did not lie. But weighing by feel follows the same principle as using a steelyard: if the counterweight is wrong, then however accurate the scale is, it will still weigh out nonsense. Big cans are compared with big cans, small cans with small cans; if you compare a small one with a big one, what you compare out is size, not sickness.”

“Being small does not mean we let it pass.” The life-or-death checks went on as before. Shake it: the water sound was right, not the rustle of sand. Press the lid: no springing back. Scrape along the seam to the bottom with a fingernail: no snag. Tilt it and count several dozen beats: not a single bead emerged from the seam.

“Reach deeper into that lower compartment and see if there are any more small ones.”

Forty-two leaned half his body in and fished out two more small cans from inside. I placed both small cans together in his palm. “Weigh them.”

He hefted them twice, and his brow loosened. “…Equal weight.”

“Equal weight is right. It is not empty; it was born this size.” I stuffed those two cans back into their original places in the compartment. “Their count will be taken when it is their turn; we will not skip around today. This can borrowed its brothers to serve once as counterweights. Counterweights do not go into the account.”

The woman at the doorway clutched the doorframe, her voice tense. “Lin Zhao, then… wouldn’t the households whose turn gets a small can suffer a loss?”

“That question reaches the root.” I said, “The greatest taboo in accounting is recording unlike things as though they were alike. A big can is recorded as ‘one can,’ and a small can is also recorded as ‘one can’; the household that draws the small can loses weight and has nowhere to argue its case. That loss would amount to something I recorded into being, and I cannot record it that way.”

I lifted the brush and added a line to the general rules: For all cans that feel light, first compare size; if sizes do not match, select another from the same compartment for comparison by hand; if the weights are equal, then inspect the seal. All cans entered into rotation shall be divided into two columns, large and small; two small cans shall count as one turn; if the final number is odd, the method of pairing must be shown to all in advance and must not be improvised on the spot. After writing it, I slowly read it aloud for the doorway to hear.

“Tonight, on the post, the turn list will be divided into two columns. Big cans in one column, small cans in one column; two small cans make one turn, and in weight no one loses to anyone. If at the very end there is an odd small can left, how it is paired will be written fixed on the list ahead of time. Rules are set up in front; no changing them halfway.”

“Those at the doorway, remember ten characters: Compare with the wrong counterweight, and a good scale tells lies. I will give you eight more: Big cans, big turns; small cans, paired turns. Take that home and pass it on.”

Forty-two reported the year as he went. When I recorded it in the page margin, I gave it an extra glance—it was not the same year as the neighboring cans on either side. “Recorded. Two streams of goods are mixed in one compartment. Tonight we will check against the old warehouse pages; perhaps we can match which year this compartment came in. Write down however much matches; if it does not match, mark it ‘provenance to be investigated.’”

“Report.”

His throat bobbed. “Fourth rack, ninth can, good!”

“Record.” The three ledgers matched. “Good thirty-four, bad sixteen, pending inspection three. Counted fifty-three.”

I glanced at the corner of the oilcloth: three charcoal circles side by side, and the cloth was still dry. The rain had sifted into mist, the thunder had retreated behind the mountains, and the white patch above the eaves had dispersed. The sky was about to clear, and I did not hurry anyone—the sky manages its business, I manage mine. Before the racks are finished, no one’s expression counts.

When Forty-two stuffed those two small cans back into the compartment, he first compared their size, then weighed them by hand, and only then let go. In one morning, his eyes had grown sharp, and a scale had risen in his hands too. In this trade, only when there is a scale in the hands can one be counted half a master.

I placed the tenth can into his cold-reddened palm.

“Compare size first, then compare weight; do not skip a single one of the old three checks.”

“Tenth can. Keep calling.”
"Fourth rack, tenth can—the lid is good, the seam is dry... but Lin Zhao, why does this can have a sour smell when you shake it?!"

I took the can from him. I did not shake it or press it yet, only held it under my nose, half a palm away, and fanned the air toward myself with my hand, once, then again.

"First, everyone stay steady. A rancid smell doesn't bite people; it bites the accounts," I said. "All along the way today, you listened for sounds, hefted weight, and looked at seams. That was eyes and hands judging the case. This time, it was the nose that sounded the alarm. The nose is also a pair of eyes on the ledger, but the case it reports has to be examined first."

"Before we examine it, let me state a principle. A sealed can is a room with no air passing through. What is smell? It is vapor. If the vapor cannot get out the door, the smell cannot get out the door either. So a sealed can gives off no smell. If you can smell rancidness, there are only two paths it could have come by: either this room has a hole, and vapor is hissing out through that hole; or this smell is not its own at all, but was rubbed onto its body. One is a capital crime; the other is bearing someone else's debt. They cannot be judged together."

I took a clean cloth, wiped the can all over, then held the cloth under my nose and fanned it to smell.

"Let the cloth judge for us."

Sour. The sourness on the cloth could not be avoided even from half a palm away.

"The smell is on the skin." I held the cloth up toward the doorway. "The inside of this can is clean; the sourness was rubbed on. A rubbed-on smell has a creditor. Which slot did it come from? Bring out the neighboring cans on the left and right."

Forty-Two leaned into the compartment and first took out the can right next to it. As soon as he pressed it, he called out himself: "It's swollen! The lid's like risen dough!"

"Handle it gently." I reached out to steady it. "It's holding a bellyful of gas. If it falls, it will burst and splash people. Put it on the table. Don't let it make a sound."

That can was placed on the oilcloth. The top of the lid was bulging, and when pressed down, it slowly bounced back, worse even than the first one from this morning. When tilted, a line of moisture hung along the bottom seam.

"We've found the creditor." I raised my voice toward the doorway. "The can just now that smelled rancid was not the culprit; it was the one reporting the case. It helped us catch this thief."

"Some of you may be muttering to yourselves: its number hadn't been called yet, so how can the neighboring one be judged first?" I shook my head. "This is not skipping numbers. This is pulling out the source of disease. If there is a fevered patient lying in a plague house, carrying him out first is not cutting the line; it is isolation. For every extra moment it lies there, its four neighbors get pickled for another moment. In the reason column of the ledger, write it clearly: source of disease removed."

That swollen can, I placed gently into the basket. "If it had slipped through today, sooner or later it would have died in someone's pot. Dying in the basket is the best end it could have."

Then we went back to inspecting the tenth can. Wiping it clean was not enough; sour liquid corrodes iron, and perhaps residue was caught in the seam. Forty-Two scraped his fingernail along the seam all the way to the end. Nothing caught. Press the lid: no bounce. Heft the weight: about the same as good goods.

"Pass. But it has been soaked in sour liquid, the same principle as that scratched can: good today is only today's good. It cannot be stored long. Put it into rotation first."

I lifted my brush and added a line to the general rules: For any can that smells rancid: first clean the body and distinguish the odor. If the cloth is rancid, the debt lies with a neighboring can; invite the neighbors for confrontation. If it remains rancid after cleaning, vapor is leaking from its own hole; scrap it. If there is a leaking can in the same compartment, first remove the source of disease; do not record it as skipping numbers. Clean and further inspect all four neighbors; if they pass, put them into rotation first. After writing, I slowly read it aloud for those at the door to hear.

"Those at the door, remember these ten words: what is sealed gives off no smell; what gives off smell is not sealed. I'll add one more sentence: when smelling a can, wave the air toward you; don't shove your nose right up against it."

"Report the total ledger. Tenth can: good, put into rotation first. One neighboring can removed, swollen lid, scrapped. Good thirty-five, bad seventeen, awaiting inspection three, checked fifty-five."

Another entry was added to the bad accounts. Out of fifty-five cans, seventeen were bad, still a little over thirty percent. The number was heavy, but I could heft it—before the count was finished, I would not allow this heart to sink to the bottom on its own.

The woman at the doorway murmured softly: "The one reporting the case..." She savored those three words twice, and her fingernail tapped lightly on the doorframe, as if she had made a note of them.

Without waiting for me to speak, Forty-Two also invited out the two remaining cans from that neighboring slot and cleaned them first. "When their numbers come, nothing is to be omitted," I said. This lad had developed a scale in his hands, and a set of rules in his heart too.

Character: You are Lin Zhao, the materials distribution administrator of “Grayridge Shelter” in the seventh year of the apocalypse, around forty years old, formerly an accountant at a grain depot before the catastrophe. Today's accounts will be settled today.

"Old Zhou's family, Zhou Youtian, three people registered under the household." I read it to her word by word. "He and his wife get two full shares. His little granddaughter Niuniu is seven, a child's half-share. Yesterday he took away two and a half tins. That half-tin was Niuniu's ration, the seventy-first entry in the accounts. The receipt is pinned right behind this page. Reach out and feel it yourself."

This question of hers touched the very string in my heart. I could not breathe a single word about the east storehouse, and precisely because of that, the number for the main storehouse had to be ironclad.

Auntie Zhao, it isn't that you don't trust me. You're afraid Xiaoshan won't make it through. But that half-tin for Niuniu is her life-saving share. … If accounts can be kneaded any way the mouth likes, this line would have broken up long ago.
I slowed my voice. “I know people are anxious. But in this line, getting anxious won’t snatch up any more, and staying steady won’t make you lose what’s yours.”
softening my voice: "Auntie Zhao, it isn't that you don't trust me.
Choose someone in the line you trust to come with me into the storehouse and count again face to face. If you count twenty-seven tins, then count these three years of work by me, Lin Zhao, as wasted.
Little Ma came running back through the muddy water, followed by Old Chen from the medical team. … "He's here."
In these three years, I haven’t let a single token come away empty-handed, and I won’t today either.
If accounts can be kneaded any way the mouth likes, this line would have broken up long ago.

stand up straight for me. … Shouting ‘I can’t trust you’ in front of the whole line isn’t shameful. In times like these, blind trust is what’s shameful.

evidence.quote: “If you really catch me writing one number short, there’s no need to make a scene. Tomorrow morning as soon as it’s light, you stand in front of this table and report that number. The written pledge on that pillar bears my fingerprint, black and white on paper: anyone may question me, and I won’t dodge a single word.”

Tearing up the paper—put before someone else’s ears, those words would be a threat; put before mine, they sounded more like something honest. A man who dared lay his words down to that extent would not doze off while counting in the afternoon.

“One more thing, so you do not glare in vain this afternoon. When we check the count, you count yours and I record mine; at the end, we compare the numbers. If they match, you make your mark beside that figure of mine. If they do not, we recount on the spot, until both you and I are convinced. By evening, your mark on the list will be right next to my seal. If you want to tear it up, the first thing you tear will be your own name.”
“Go back and eat your midday meal properly. Counting is work that wears out the eyes. I will not accept numbers counted on an empty stomach.”

“On that sheet of paper, every stroke is the count of two hundred people. The dozens of households at the back of the line who know only a few characters rely on it being nailed to the pillar, still there through sun and rain. If you tear it up on their behalf, when they turn around and ask whose turn it is, who will answer? You will have vented your anger, yes, but you will also have gouged out their eyes.”

“All right. Since you’ve accepted the errand, don’t shrink back.” I lifted the brush again. “Go back and eat your midday meal properly. Counting is work that wears out the eyes. I will not accept numbers counted on an empty stomach.”

In my heart, that ring of keys sank another degree. If those three pairs of eyes this afternoon counted out a bad number... then a bad number would have to be written down too. This written pledge had nailed even me to the pillar; that was what it was meant to nail in the first place.

evidence.quote: “Remember one thing: what you should be watching isn't me as a person, but the numbers.”
“Twenty-six cans in the main storehouse; one can taken out by approval slip; twenty-five cans remaining go into the rotation. From this moment on, the number that counts is twenty-five.”
“Put your tag on the desk. State your tag number, how many people in your household—one thing at a time.”

That was the one word I gave in answer. Right now that force in him was aimed at me; by afternoon it would have to be aimed at the numbers. It was a good force, and it needed a proper place to be put to use.

Someone in the line muttered, “One less can again...”

“It isn't less; it was reserved in advance.”

My heart sank a little. Old Chen did not issue slips lightly; if one had been issued, then the child really had burned to that point. But this heaviness was better than the suspense of this morning. Suspense meant having no count; heaviness meant having a count.

What he trusts is no longer the sheet of paper nailed to the pillar, but the East Warehouse he is about to check with his own hands—because those numbers will pass through his eyes, be reported from his mouth, and be written by his hand into the turn sheet, becoming part of himself.
Save your eyes for counting this afternoon. Don't burn them dry first at my table. Go back and get something hot to eat. At the wei hour, under the post.”
this can for Xiaoshan was given by the rules, not as a favor bestowed by anyone.

“One more thing. Since everyone is here, remember this. From the last two entries yesterday, the receipts have not been handed back. Whose families they are, I know in my heart; I won't name them here. Before the line disperses, deliver them to this table. They will be needed to balance the accounts tonight. If you cannot deliver them, I will step through the mud to your door to fetch them. I will still get them all the same—it will just cost me lamp oil.”

Appoint the sharpest questioner as the team’s supervision representative for the East Warehouse inspection, turning their suspicion into a collective supervisory responsibility and achieving a leap in the trust structure from “guarding against my breaking faith” to “co-witnessing credibility.”
The words have become paper, and the paper has become nails; there is no further risk of inconsistency.
The credit accumulated over three years has become a weight on the scale, and now even the beam has been nailed to the pillar; the whole team can see where the star is.

evidence.quote: “And to be plain about it, if you’re afraid I’ll alter the accounts, what exactly are you afraid of?” I pushed his rations neatly toward the edge of the table. “The rule is that what’s issued can’t be taken back. The grain is in your arms, the can is in your hands. Even if I wanted to change it, what could I change it to?
“Go on, take a look. It’s only two rows of sheds away, a few steps along the muddy path. But remember three things.”

when you come back, tell it exactly as it is. If the children have eaten, say they’ve eaten; if they haven’t, say they haven’t. Good words or bad, you’re not allowed to add or subtract a thing. Tonight the whole team will be asking what those eyes of yours saw. From this afternoon on, that mouth of yours counts for half the notice on the pillar.”
If I really meant to alter the accounts, I wouldn’t pick today. Today, around this table, there are more eyes than there are cans in the storehouse.”

"If the sky changes before the wei hour, the inspection will be moved up. I'll have Xiaoma call along the line and gather everyone under the pillar. You—if you hear the call from the third row east, don't look around; just run back as fast as you can."

After writing that entry, I stared at it myself for quite a while. In the morning the ledger had been broken; I had gone into the storehouse empty-handed to count the stock. Now the receipts were complete, and when the accounts were checked back, twenty-six matched twenty-six, fitting perfectly. The ledger and the goods in the storehouse had locked together at both ends.
From this moment on, the accounts of the main storehouse were complete. What remained was to wait for those three pairs of eyes at the wei hour.

evidence.quote: This question carried more weight than thunder. Asking “whose head does it count against” meant those pairs of ears at the door had already started thinking against the accounts; once people start thinking against the accounts, panic can be held down. This question was worth my stopping the whole rack’s numbers and answering it piece by piece.
Hidden inside that question are two questions. I’ll split them apart. One: if this tin really has gone bad, whose loss is it? Two: if it’s judged wrong, whose responsibility is it?
There are also people muttering in their hearts: if we balance the accounts today, how can they be balanced with the word ‘pending’ hanging there?

It doesn’t count against anyone. It hasn’t been issued into anyone’s hands, so it can’t take up anyone’s allotment; it hasn’t entered the rotation, so it can’t crowd out anyone’s turn. It counts against last night’s rain.

Three columns: good, bad, pending inspection. Add the three columns together, and they equal the total inspected, not one piece off—that is balanced. ‘Pending’ is also a number. Once it falls into ink, it is no longer hanging.
One sound in exchange for one belly—that trade is no loss.

You come first thing tomorrow morning. The cloth was laid out while you watched me, and the circle was drawn in front of you. You watch with your own eyes which column this entry is moved into from ‘pending,’ then check it against the pillar, and the pillar against the basket. When all three places bite together, this tin will have a beginning and an end.
The front and back pages bite into each other; it can’t run away.
In the accounts it will be recorded: first tin of the fourth rack, pending inspection, transferred to scrap.

“Shortfall: count it under the rain’s account.”

“Miscount: count it under the signers’ account.”

Cans awaiting inspection: cloth dry, enter as good; cloth wet, enter as bad. Those that turn bad are recorded under the rain account, not under any person’s account and not under any turn. If inspection is wrong, the three signers bear it together.

The same question had been asked twice within the time it takes an incense stick to burn. … The problem is on my side: my answer was long, and the rain can wash it away. This time I’ll give you the short version, short enough that the rain can’t wash it away.
All of you come in under the eaves. Don’t stand in the rain asking about accounts.
This question is being asked a second time, and I am not angry. If you are willing to ask, it means you are looking at the accounts and thinking. That is a good thing.
From now on, if anyone asks this question again, there is no need to brave the rain and crowd to the warehouse door. You will be carrying the answer in your own mouths.
Twelve characters, two sentences: "Shortfall, count it to the rain." "Miscount, count it to the pawn."
“You, the one who asked just now.” … “These twelve words—shout them once to the people behind you. Once you shout them out, this answer belongs to all of you, not to my counter.”

Giving it only by mouth was still not enough. I opened the notes at the very front of the ledger … I lifted my brush and, in front of the several pairs of eyes at the door, wrote:

Cans awaiting inspection
Tonight this rule will also be copied onto the pillar, nailed up together with the turns and the bad count.
This rule is not being set only for the can in front of us. From now on, any can we are unsure about will be handled according to this. Set the rule once, and it saves answering again every time.

evidence.quote: “Canned goods are not made with the expectation that people will rush to eat them the day they leave the factory. Before the disaster I kept accounts at the grain station. There was an old saying passed down over the counter: the date is its birthday; the seal is its life. When you check a household register, you check the birthday; when you inspect goods, you inspect the life.”

If you really want to talk about the poison line, there is only one: did dirty water get in or not. Whether it got in is not determined by what year it was born in, but by whether the seal has confessed.

This question was even more worth pausing over than that cry of “rusted through.” A swollen lid and seepage—everyone knew that meant bad. But the three words “old date” were something everyone understood, yet no one was quite sure about; they were the easiest thing to ride the sound of the rain and burrow into people’s hearts.

“As for why its date is earlier than last month’s, the source is different.” … This batch from the East Storehouse is old reserve stock, accumulated in the first few years. When it was stored, no one looked at the date; they looked at the seal. Old is its provenance, not its illness.”

“But that glance of yours has reminded me. From now on we add half a rule: when handling each can, glance at the year while you’re at it. Don’t enter it in the good-or-bad column; just call it out. … For those that don’t, the list will carry the four words ‘source pending investigation.’ Same principle as that can set upside down: leaving it hanging and unspoken is the hole; once it falls into ink, it no longer hangs.”

In my heart I weighed that fifteen. Out of forty-seven cans, fifteen bad—just over thirty percent. That number was heavy, but heavy was better than hanging—hanging meant having no number; heavy meant having a number. The counting was not finished, and I would not allow myself to collapse first.
Those at the door, record ten words: the date is its birthday; the seal is its life. Pass that on when you go home.
“This can,” I looked back at Forty-Two, “you pressed it and felt it; I checked it again. All three checks are complete. Report.”
I put the fourth can from the fourth rack into the palm of Forty-Two Frozen Red's hand. Keep going. Glance at the year as you go; don't hold up the count.
From the disaster to today, it has been a full seven years. In these seven years, which can that has gone into anyone’s belly did not have a pre-disaster date? … Not once was the date to blame.

From now on we add half a rule: … For those that don’t, the list will carry the four words ‘source pending investigation.’ Same principle as that can set upside down: leaving it hanging and unspoken is the hole; once it falls into ink, it no longer hangs.

"Those at the door, remember these ten words: what is sealed gives off no smell; what gives off smell is not sealed. I'll add one more sentence: when smelling a can, wave the air toward you; don't shove your nose right up against it."

I lifted my brush and added a line to the general rules: For any can that smells rancid: first clean the body and distinguish the odor. If the cloth is rancid, the debt lies with a neighboring can; invite the neighbors for confrontation. If it remains rancid after cleaning, vapor is leaking from its own hole; scrap it. If there is a leaking can in the same compartment, first remove the source of disease; do not record it as skipping numbers. Clean and further inspect all four neighbors; if they pass, put them into rotation first.
Without waiting for me to speak, Forty-Two also invited out the two remaining cans from that neighboring slot and cleaned them first. "When their numbers come, nothing is to be omitted," I said.
